available at extra charge

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter for each answer.

transcript.text: Good morning, Clare House Hotel.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: Andrew speaking.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: I’m the Events Manager.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: Good morning, Andrew.
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: My name’s Samantha.
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: I’m arranging a party for my parents’ fiftieth wedding anniversary, and I’m ringing to ask about hiring a room some time next September.
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: Also my parents and several of the guests will need accommodation.
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: OK, I’m sure we can help you with that.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: Will you be having a sit-down meal or a buffet?
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: Probably a sit-down.
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: And do you know how many people there’ll be?
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: Around eighty, I think.
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: Well we have two rooms that can hold that number.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: One is the Adelphi Room.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: That can seat eighty-five, or hold over a hundred if people are standing for a buffet.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: If you have live music, there’s room for four or five musicians in the gallery overlooking the room.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: Our guests usually appreciate the fact that the music can be loud enough for dancing, but not too loud for conversation.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: Yes, I really don’t like it when you can’t talk.
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: Exactly.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: Now the Adelphi Room is at the back of the hotel, and there are French windows leading out onto the terrace.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: This has a beautiful display of pots of roses at that time of the year.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: Which direction does it face?
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: Southwest, so that side of the hotel gets the sun in the afternoon and early evening.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: Very nice.
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: From the terrace you can see the area of trees within the grounds of the hotel, or you can stroll through there to the river – that’s on the far side, so it isn’t visible from the hotel.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: Then another option is the Carlton Room.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: This is a bit bigger – it can hold up to a hundred and ten people – and it has the advantage of a stage, which is useful if you have any entertainment, or indeed a small band can fit onto it.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: And can you go outside from the room?
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: No, the Carlton Room is on the first floor, but on one side the windows look out onto the lake.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: Lovely.
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: I think either of those rooms would be suitable.
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: Can I tell you about some of the options we offer in addition?
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: Please do.
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: As well as a meal, you can have an MC, a Master of Ceremonies, who’ll be with you throughout the party.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: What exactly is the MC’s function?
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: I suppose they make a speech during the meal if we need one, do they?
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: All our MCs are trained as public speakers, so they can easily get people’s attention – many guests are glad to have someone who can make themselves heard above the chatter!
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: And they’re also your support – if anything goes wrong, the MC will deal with it, so you can relax.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: Great!
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: I’ll need to ask you about food, but something else that’s important is accommodation.
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: You obviously have rooms in the hotel, but do you also have any other accommodation, like cabins, for example?
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: Yes, there are five in the grounds, all self-contained.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: They each sleep two to four people and have their own living room, bathroom and small kitchen.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: That sounds perfect for what we’ll need.
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: Now you have various facilities, don’t you?
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: Are they all included in the price of hiring the room?
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: The pool, for instance.
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: Normally you’d be able to use it, but it’ll be closed throughout September for refurbishment, I’m afraid.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: The gym will be available, though, at no extra charge.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: That’s open all day, from six in the morning until midnight.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: And the tennis courts, but there is a small additional payment for those.
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: We have four courts, and it’s worth booking in advance if you possibly can, as there can be quite a long waiting list for them!
transcript.speaker: ANDREW

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: Now could we discuss the food?
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: This would be dinner, around seven o’clock …
transcript.speaker: SAM

transcript.text: Hello everyone.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I’m Jake Stevens and I’m your rep here at the hotel.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I’m sure you’ll all have a great time here.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: So let me tell you a bit about what’s on offer.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I’ll start by telling you about some of the excursions that are available for guests.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: One thing you have to do while you’re here is go dolphin watching.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: On our boat trips, we pretty well guarantee you’ll see dolphins – if you don’t you can repeat the trip free of charge.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We organise daily trips for just 35 euros.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Unfortunately there aren’t any places left for this afternoon’s trip, but come and see me to book for later in the week.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: If you’re energetic, I’d recommend our forest walk.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s a guided walk of about seven kilometres.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: There’ll be a stop half way, and you’ll be provided with a drink and sandwiches.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: There’s some fairly steep climbs up the hills, so you need to be reasonably fit for this one, with good shoes, and bring a waterproof in case it rains.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s just 25 euros all inclusive, and it’s every Wednesday.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Then on Thursdays we organise a cycle trip, which will give you all the fun of biking without the effort.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’ll take you and your bike up to the top of Mount Larna, and leave you to bike back – it’s a 700-metre drop in just 20 kilometres so this isn’t really for inexperienced cyclists as you’ll be going pretty fast.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: And if it’s a clear day, you’ll have fantastic views.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: On our local craft tour you can find out about the traditional activities in the island.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: And the best thing about this trip is that it’s completely free.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: You’ll be taken to a factory where jewellery is made, and also a ceramics centre.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: If you want, you can buy some of the products but that’s entirely up to you.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The trip starts after lunch on Thursday, and you’ll return by 6 pm.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: If you’re interested in astronomy you may already know that the island’s one of the best places in the world to observe the night sky.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We can offer trips to the observatory on Friday for those who are interested.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: They cost 90 euros per person and you’ll be shown the huge telescopes and have a talk from an expert, who’ll explain all about how they work.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Afterwards we’ll head down to Sunset Beach, where you can have a dip in the ocean if you want before we head off back to the hotel.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Finally, there’s horse riding.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: This is organised by the Equestrian Centre over near Playa Cortino and it’s a great experience if you’re a keen horseback rider, or even if you’ve never been on a horse before.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: They take you down to the beach, and you can canter along the sand and through the waves.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It costs 35 euros and it’s available every day.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: So there’s plenty to do in the daytime, but what about night life?
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Well, the number one attraction’s called ‘Musical Favourites’.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Guests enjoy a three-course meal and unlimited free drinks, and watch a fantastic show, starting with musicals set in Paris and then crossing the Atlantic to Las Vegas and finally Copacabana.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: At the end the cast members come down from the stage, still in their stunning costumes, and you’ll have a chance to chat with them. It’s hugely popular, so let me know now if you’re interested because it’s no good leaving it until the last minute.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s on Friday night.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Tickets are just 50 euros each, but for an extra 10 euros you can have a table right by the stage.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: If you’d like to go back in time, there’s the Castle Feast on Saturday evening.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s held in a twelfth-century castle, and you eat in the great courtyard, with ladies in long gowns serving your food.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: You’re given a whole chicken each, which you eat in the medieval way, using your hands instead of cutlery, and you’re entertained by competitions where the horseback riders attempt to knock one another off their horses. Then you can watch the dancers in the ballroom and join in as well if you want.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: OK, so now if anyone …
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Hello, Trevor.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: Hello, Stephanie.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: You said you wanted to talk about the course I’m taking on literature for children.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: I’m thinking of doing it next year, but I’d like to find out more about it first.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: OK, well, as you probably know, it’s a one-year course.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: It’s divided into six modules, and you have to take all of them.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: One of the most interesting ones, for me, at least, was about the purpose of children’s literature.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: You mean, whether it should just entertain children or should be educational, as well.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: Right, and whether the teaching should be factual – giving them information about the world – or ethical, teaching them values.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: What’s fascinating is that the writer isn’t necessarily conscious of the message they’re conveying.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: For instance, a story might show a child who has a problem as a result of not doing what an adult has told them to do, implying that children should always obey adults.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: I see what you mean.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: That module made me realise how important stories are – they can have a significant effect on children as they grow up.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: Actually, it inspired me to have a go at it myself, just for my own interest.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: I know I can’t compete with the really popular stories, like the Harry Potter books – they’re very good, and even young kids like my seven-year-old niece love reading them.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: Mm.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: I’m very interested in illustrations in stories.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: Is that covered in the course?
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: Yes, there’s a module on pictures, and how they’re sometimes central to the story.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: That’s good.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: I remember some frightening ones I saw as a child and I can still see them vividly in my mind, years later!
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: Pictures can be so powerful, just as powerful as words.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: I’ve always enjoyed drawing, so that’s the field I want to go into when I finish the course.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: I bet that module will be really helpful.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: I’m sure it will.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: We also studied comics in that module, but I’m not convinced of their value, not compared with books.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: One of the great things about words is that you use your imagination, but with a comic you don’t have to.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: But children are so used to visual input – on TV, video games, and so on.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: There are plenty of kids who wouldn’t even try to read a book, so I think comics can serve a really useful purpose.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: You mean, it’s better to read a comic than not to read at all?
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: Yes, I suppose you’re right.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: I just think it’s sad when children don’t read books.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: What about books for girls and books for boys?
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: Does the course go into that?
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: Yes, there’s a module on it.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: For years, lots of stories, in English, at least, assumed that boys went out and did adventurous things and girls stayed at home and played with dolls.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: I was amazed how many books were targeted at just one sex or the other.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: Of course this reflects society as it is when the books are written.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: That’s true.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: So it sounds as though you think it’s a good course.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: Definitely.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: Have you been reading lots of children’s stories, to help you decide whether to take the course?
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: Yeah.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: I’ve gone as far back as the late seventeenth century, though I know there were earlier children’s stories.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: So does that mean you’ve read Perrault’s fairy tales?
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: Cinderella, The Sleeping Beauty, and so on.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: They must be important, because no stories of that type had been written before, they were the first.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: Then there’s The Swiss Family Robinson.
transcript.speaker: STEPHANIE

transcript.text: I haven’t read that.
transcript.speaker: TREVOR

transcript.text: The English name makes it sound as though Robinson is the family’s surname, but a more accurate translation would be The Swiss Robinsons, because it’s about a Swiss family who are shipwrecked, like Robinson Crusoe in the novel of a century earlier.

groups.title: The hunt for sunken settlements and ancient shipwrecks
groups.instruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

transcript.text: In today’s class I’m going to talk about marine archaeology, the branch of archaeology focusing on human interaction with the sea, lakes and rivers.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It’s the study of ships, cargoes, shipping facilities, and other physical remains.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: I’ll give you an example, then go on to show how this type of research is being transformed by the use of the latest technology.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Atlit-Yam was a village on the coast of the eastern Mediterranean, which seems to have been thriving until around 7,000 BC.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The residents kept cattle, caught fish and stored grain.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: They had wells for fresh water, many of their houses were built around a courtyard and were constructed of stone.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The village contained an impressive monument: seven half-tonne stones standing in a semicircle around a spring, that might have been used for ceremonial purposes.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Atlit-Yam may have been destroyed swiftly by a tsunami, or climate change may have caused glaciers to melt and sea levels to rise, flooding the village gradually.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Whatever the cause, it now lies ten metres below the surface of the Mediterranean, buried under sand at the bottom of the sea.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It’s been described as the largest and best preserved prehistoric settlement ever found on the seabed.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For marine archaeologists, Atlit-Yam is a treasure trove.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Research on the buildings, tools and the human remains has revealed how the bustling village once functioned, and even what diseases some of its residents suffered from.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But of course this is only one small village, one window into a lost world.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For a fuller picture, researchers need more sunken settlements, but the hard part is finding them.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Underwater research used to require divers to find shipwrecks or artefacts, but in the second half of the twentieth century, various types of underwater vehicles were developed, some controlled from a ship on the surface, and some of them autonomous, which means they don’t need to be operated by a person.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Autonomous underwater vehicles, or AUVs, are used in the oil industry, for instance, to create maps of the seabed before rigs and pipelines are installed.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: To navigate they use sensors, such as compasses and sonar.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Until relatively recently they were very expensive, and so heavy that they had to be launched from a large vessel with a winch.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But the latest AUVs are much easier to manoeuvre – they can be launched from the shore or a small ship.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And they’re much cheaper, which makes them more accessible to research teams.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: They’re also very sophisticated.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: They can communicate with each other and, for example, work out the most efficient way to survey a site, or to find particular objects on the seabed.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Field tests show the approach can work.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For example, in a trial in 2015, three AUVs searched for wrecks at Marzamemi, off the coast of Sicily.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The site is the final resting place of an ancient Roman ship, which sank in the sixth century AD while ferrying prefabricated marble elements for the construction of an early church.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The AUVs mapped the area in detail, finding other ships carrying columns of the same material.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Creating an internet in the sea for AUVs to communicate is no easy matter.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Wifi networks on land use electromagnetic waves, but in water these will only travel a few centimetres.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Instead, a more complex mix of technologies is required.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For short distances, AUVs can share data using light, while acoustic waves are used to communicate over long distances.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But more creative solutions are also being developed, where an AUV working on the seabed offloads data to a second AUV, which then surfaces and beams the data home to the research team using a satellite.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: There’s also a system that enables AUVs to share information from seabed scans, and other data.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So if an AUV surveying the seabed finds an intriguing object, it can share the coordinates of the object – that is, its position – with a nearby AUV that carries superior cameras, and arrange for that AUV to make a closer inspection of the object.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Marine archaeologists are excited about the huge potential of these AUVs for their discipline.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: One site where they’re going to be deployed is the Gulf of Baratti, off the Italian coast.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In 1974, a 2,000-year-old Roman vessel was discovered here, in 18 metres of water.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: When it sank, it was carrying medical goods, in wooden or tin receptacles.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Its cargo gives us insight into the treatments available all those years ago, including tablets that are thought to have been dissolved to form a cleansing liquid for the eyes.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Other Roman ships went down nearby, taking their cargoes with them.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Some held huge pots made of terracotta.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Some were used for transporting cargoes of olive oil, and others held wine.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In many cases it’s only these containers that remain, while the wooden ships have been buried under silt on the seabed.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Another project that’s about to …
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
